3. Get to know the data

3.1 There are 93 rows and 14 columns, and each row is a different penguin

penguins |> count(species)

4. Filter and remove outliers
4.1
```{r}
penguins |> ggplot(data = penguins,
       mapping = aes(x = wing.length,
                     y = beak.length_culmen,
                     colour = genus)) +
  geom_point()
```

Mainly the orange points (aptenodytes). Some yellow (eudyptes), but most yellow are within the range of the majority.

4.2 

```{r}
penguins |> filter(wing.length > 150 & beak.length_culmen < 60) |> head() #I would say that they are all Eudyptes as I had described before, and just three penguins
```

A tibble: 3 × 14
  species           genus shortname sex   beak.length_culmen beak.length_nares
  <chr>             <chr> <chr>     <chr>              <dbl>             <dbl>
1 Eudyptes pachyrh… Eudy… E. pachy… F                   47.3              33.5
2 Eudyptes pachyrh… Eudy… E. pachy… F                   46.7              35.5
3 Eudyptes pachyrh… Eudy… E. pachy… M                   55.4              39.8

#I saw that you asked for species, and for 4 outliers, so I guess for the next question I should re-do the 4.2 and consider one of the Aptenodytes as a outlier as well

```{r}
penguins |> filter(wing.length > 150 & beak.length_culmen < 70) |> head()
```

4.3
```{r}
penguins_clean <- penguins |> select(species, genus, wing.length, beak.length_culmen) |> na.omit(wing.length=NA) |> filter(!(wing.length > 150 & beak.length_culmen < 70))
```

#I removed the outliers because aside from being different from the "main" population, they were also very different from their species.

5.Draft figure
```{r}
penguins_clean |> ggplot(data = penguins_clean,
       mapping = aes(x = wing.length,
                     y = beak.length_culmen,
                     colour = genus)) +
  geom_point()
```

#As we can see from the ggplot, the penguins that seem to have higher beak lenght seem to also have higher wingh lenght, being conserved within each species, which make sense because we expect that "bigger" penguins have bigger wings and bigger beaks.

6.Summarise by species

```{r}
species_summary <- penguins_clean |> group_by(species, genus) |> summarise(n = n(),
          mean_wing_length = mean(wing.length, na.rm = TRUE),
          mean_beak_length = mean(beak.length_culmen, na.rm = TRUE))

species_summary
```

```{r}
ggplot(data = species_summary,
       mapping = aes(x = mean_wing_length,
                     y = mean_beak_length,
                     colour = genus)) +
                   labs(title = "Species summary final exercise",
       x = "mean_wing_length (mm)",
       y = "mean_beak_length (mm)",
       colour = "genus") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")) +
  geom_point()
```
